slides.title: Fundamental Design Patterns I: Creational and Structural Patterns
slides.speakerNotes: Welcome to our exploration of design patterns. Today we focus on two categories: creational patterns (how we create objects) and structural patterns (how we compose objects). These are foundational tools that every software engineer should master. Set the stage by emphasizing that patterns are not just academic concepts but practical solutions used daily in industry.

slides.title: What Are Design Patterns?

blocks.content: Reusable solutions to commonly occurring problems in software design

items: Templates, not finished code—adapt to context
Capture decades of expert knowledge
Shared vocabulary for design communication
Balance flexibility, reusability, and complexity

content.title: Pattern Recognition Challenge
content.instructions: Examine this code snippet: A Logger class with a private constructor, static getInstance() method, and single instance variable. What design problem does this solve? What pattern might this be? What trade-offs does this approach introduce?
content.format: Think-pair-share: 1 min individual, 1 min discuss with neighbor, 1 min class discussion

slides.speakerNotes: After presenting the definition and analogy, engage students in analyzing a real pattern implementation before formally introducing patterns. The Logger example is a Singleton (covered in slide 4), but here students diagnose the design intent and trade-offs. This activates analyze-level thinking: identifying the problem being solved, recognizing the solution structure, and evaluating consequences. Use responses to preview that patterns solve specific problems but introduce trade-offs—foreshadowing the evaluation skills needed for pattern selection. Collect answers via polling or volunteers.

slides.title: Pattern Categories: Analyzing Design Intent

content.prompt: Hierarchical diagram with three colored boxes: 'Creational Patterns' (blue) showing Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory with 'Controls object creation'; 'Structural Patterns' (green) showing Adapter, Composite, Decorator with 'Organizes object composition'; 'Behavioral Patterns' (gray) with 'Next Lecture' label. content.title: Pattern Category Diagnosis
content.instructions: Analyze these scenarios and identify which pattern category applies: (1) You need multiple database connection objects to share the same configuration. (2) You want to add logging behavior to existing classes without modifying them. (3) You need a tree structure where individual items and groups are treated uniformly. Justify your category choice based on the design problem.
content.format: Poll responses, then discuss reasoning for each scenario

slides.speakerNotes: The Gang of Four (1994) formalized 23 patterns into three categories based on design intent. Today covers 6 patterns across creational and structural categories. Use the activity to engage analyze-level thinking: students must diagnose the core design problem (object creation vs. composition) and map it to the appropriate category. Scenario 1 is creational (shared creation logic), 2 is structural (adding behavior through composition), 3 is structural (uniform treatment via composition). Collect poll responses and discuss how recognizing design intent guides pattern selection—foreshadowing evaluation skills needed later.

slides.title: Singleton Pattern: Ensuring One Instance

items: Intent: One instance, global access
Private constructor blocks external creation
Static method controls access
Use for coordinating system-wide actions

content.prompt: UML class diagram showing Singleton class with: private static instance variable, private constructor, public static getInstance() method returning the instance. Show the self-reference arrow from getInstance to the instance.

slides.speakerNotes: Singleton ensures exactly one instance exists. Classic examples: configuration manager, logger, connection pool. The key mechanism: private constructor prevents external instantiation, static method provides controlled access. Draw attention to the self-referential nature—the class manages its own unique instance. Mention lazy vs. eager initialization strategies.

slides.title: Singleton Implementation: Design Analysis

content.title: Analyze & Evaluate
content.instructions: Examine this implementation and answer: (1) Why is volatile necessary? What happens without it? (2) Identify one scenario where this Singleton creates problems for testing. (3) Would you use this pattern for a cache manager in a microservices architecture? Justify your answer.
content.format: Think-pair-share: 1 min individual, 1 min pairs, 1 min class discussion

items: ✓ Thread-safe, lazy initialization, low overhead
✗ Hidden dependencies, testing difficulties
✗ Global state complicates distributed systems
Alternative: Dependency injection for testability

slides.speakerNotes: Guide students through analyzing the double-checked locking mechanism—volatile ensures memory visibility preventing partially constructed objects. During activity, listen for: testing issues (mocking difficulties, global state), distributed system concerns (instance per JVM, not truly global). Highlight that pattern choice requires evaluating context: acceptable for desktop app configuration, problematic for distributed cache. Emphasize that recognizing when NOT to use a pattern is as important as knowing how to implement it. Transition to Factory Method as alternative approach to controlled instantiation.

slides.title: Factory Method Pattern: Application & Analysis

content.title: Apply Factory Method
content.instructions: Design problem: You're building a notification system that sends alerts via Email, SMS, or Push. The NotificationService class needs to create the right notifier based on user preferences, but shouldn't depend on concrete notifier classes. Sketch: (1) Which classes/interfaces you'd create, (2) Where the factory method goes, (3) How subclasses provide specific notifiers. Then evaluate: Would simple if-else in one class be better? Why or why not?
content.format: 2 min individual sketch, 2 min pair discussion of trade-offs

content.prompt: UML class diagram showing Creator abstract class with factoryMethod():Product and sendNotification(), ConcreteCreatorEmail/SMS/Push extending Creator, Notifier interface, and EmailNotifier/SMSNotifier/PushNotifier implementing Notifier. Highlight factoryMethod() returns Notifier type.

items: Use when: Creation logic varies by context/subclass
Use when: Framework defines structure, apps provide specifics
Avoid when: Only one product type (over-engineering)
Avoid when: Creation logic simple and stable (use DI instead)

slides.speakerNotes: Guide students through applying Factory Method to notification problem. Listen for correct identification: NotificationService as Creator with createNotifier() factory method, subclasses for each channel. During evaluation, push students to justify: Factory Method adds complexity (parallel hierarchies) but gains extensibility and testability. Simple if-else might suffice for stable requirements, but Factory Method supports Open/Closed when new notification types emerge. Emphasize that pattern choice requires analyzing requirements—stability vs. extensibility, simplicity vs. flexibility. Connect to next slide's logistics example showing similar structure in different domain.

slides.title: Factory Method: Apply & Analyze

content.title: Implement Factory Method
content.instructions: You're extending a logistics system that currently handles Road and Sea transport. Add Air transport support. On paper: (1) Write the AirLogistics subclass with createTransport() method, (2) Sketch the Plane class implementing Transport, (3) Identify which parts you modified vs. extended. Then analyze: What if you had used a simple static factory instead? What would change when adding new transport types?
content.format: 3 min implementation, 2 min pair comparison of Factory Method vs. static factory trade-offs

items: Analyze: Which classes changed? Which were extended?
Compare: Static factory vs. Factory Method for this scenario
Evaluate: Is the parallel hierarchy justified here?
When would simpler approach suffice?

slides.speakerNotes: Guide students through extending the logistics system with Air transport. This apply-level task requires implementing the pattern, not just recognizing it. During analysis, emphasize Open/Closed Principle: adding AirLogistics extends without modifying existing code. Push students to evaluate trade-offs: Factory Method adds complexity through parallel hierarchies but enables extension without modification. Static factory would require modifying existing code for each new type. Connect to slide 6's notification system showing similar extension scenario. Highlight that pattern choice depends on anticipated change—stable requirements favor simplicity, expected growth favors Factory Method.

slides.title: Abstract Factory: Creating Product Families

items: Intent: Create families of related objects
Ensures products work together
Multiple creation methods per factory
Client uses abstract interfaces only

content.prompt: UML diagram showing AbstractFactory interface with createProductA() and createProductB() methods, ConcreteFactory1 and ConcreteFactory2 implementing it, AbstractProductA and AbstractProductB interfaces, and concrete products ProductA1, ProductA2, ProductB1, ProductB2. Use different colors for each product family.

slides.speakerNotes: Abstract Factory creates families of related objects. Key difference from Factory Method: creates multiple product types that must work together. Classic example: UI toolkit creating Button, Checkbox, ScrollBar for Windows/Mac/Linux—products from same family share consistent look. The factory interface declares creation methods for each product type. Concrete factories return compatible products. Client code works only with abstract interfaces, never concrete classes.

slides.title: Abstract Factory vs Factory Method

items: Abstract Factory: object composition, creates product families
Factory Method: inheritance, creates single products
Abstract Factory often uses Factory Methods internally
Adding product types: affects all factories (limitation)
Adding product families: just add new factory (strength)

blocks.content: Use Abstract Factory when products must be used together consistently

slides.speakerNotes: Critical comparison: Factory Method uses inheritance (subclasses decide), Abstract Factory uses composition (factory objects decide). Abstract Factory handles product families—multiple related products. Factory Method handles single product hierarchies. Abstract Factory is often implemented using Factory Methods for each product. Trade-off: adding new product types requires changing all factory interfaces, but adding new product families is easy—just create new concrete factory. Example: adding 'TextField' to UI toolkit requires updating all platform factories.

slides.title: Adapter Pattern: Interface Conversion

items: Intent: Convert incompatible interfaces
Wraps existing class with new interface
Two variants: Class and Object Adapter
Enables reuse without modification

content.prompt: UML diagram showing Client using Target interface, Adapter implementing Target and containing Adaptee reference, and Adaptee class with incompatible interface. Show delegation arrow from Adapter to Adaptee with 'adaptee.specificRequest()' label.

slides.speakerNotes: Adapter makes incompatible interfaces work together—like a power adapter converting US plug to European socket. The Adapter implements the interface the client expects (Target) and wraps the existing class (Adaptee). Object Adapter uses composition (shown here)—more flexible, can adapt multiple adaptees. Class Adapter uses multiple inheritance—more efficient but less flexible. Real example: Java's InputStreamReader adapts byte streams to character streams. Use when you can't modify existing code but need it to work with new interface.

slides.title: Adapter Pattern: Apply & Analyze

content.text:
**Design Challenge**: Your system uses `Logger` interface with `log(String msg)`. A third-party library provides `AdvancedLogger` with `writeLog(String msg, LogLevel level, Timestamp time)`. You need structured logging with levels and timestamps, but can't modify either interface.

**Task**: Design an adapter solution. What goes in the adapter? How does it bridge the interfaces?

content.instructions: 1. Complete the adapter (1 min). 2. Pair: Compare solutions—what assumptions did you make about log level and timestamp? (1 min). 3. Analyze: What are the trade-offs of your design choices? When would this adapter fail? (1 min)

slides.speakerNotes: This apply-level activity has students design an adapter for a realistic scenario. Key learning: adapters often add logic (default LogLevel, current timestamp) beyond simple delegation. During pair discussion, surface different approaches: some hardcode INFO level, others parse message for level indicators. Analysis phase targets evaluate level: trade-offs include loss of caller control over level/timestamp vs. simplicity. Adapter fails if client needs fine-grained control—this reveals pattern limitations. Debrief by showing one solution, then discuss when to use Class Adapter (multiple inheritance) vs. Object Adapter (composition) based on their designs. Connect to objective: applying structural patterns to solve composition problems with justified design choices.

slides.title: Composite Pattern: Part-Whole Hierarchies

items: Intent: Compose objects into tree structures
Treat individual and composite objects uniformly
Recursive composition
Component, Leaf, Composite roles

content.prompt: UML diagram showing Component interface with operation(), Leaf implementing Component, and Composite implementing Component with children list and add/remove methods. Show tree structure with Composite containing both Leaf and other Composite objects.

slides.speakerNotes: Composite represents part-whole hierarchies as trees. Classic example: file system with files (leaves) and directories (composites containing files and other directories). The key insight: clients treat leaves and composites uniformly through Component interface. Composite stores children and delegates operations to them recursively. This enables building complex structures from simple parts. The pattern embodies recursion—composites can contain other composites. GUI frameworks use this extensively: panels contain buttons, labels, and other panels.

slides.title: Composite Pattern: Implementation Challenge

content.title: Apply & Analyze (3 min)
content.instructions:
1. Complete the draw() method using recursive delegation
2. Decide: Should add/remove methods be in Graphic interface or only CompositeGraphic?
3. Justify your choice: What are the trade-offs?

Consider: What happens if client calls add() on a Circle?
content.deliverable: Code completion + design decision with rationale

slides.speakerNotes: This active learning exercise elevates engagement to apply and analyze levels. Students first apply the pattern by implementing recursive delegation, then analyze the transparency vs. safety trade-off. Poll students on their interface decision. Transparency (add/remove in Graphic) treats all objects uniformly but allows unsafe operations on leaves. Safety (add/remove only in Composite) prevents errors but requires type checking. Discuss how different contexts favor different approaches: GUI frameworks often choose transparency, while type-safe systems prefer safety. Connect to real design decisions they'll face.

slides.title: Decorator Pattern: Dynamic Responsibilities

items: Intent: Add responsibilities dynamically
Flexible alternative to subclassing
Decorator wraps component
Multiple decorators can be stacked

content.prompt: UML diagram showing Component interface, ConcreteComponent implementing it, Decorator implementing Component and containing Component reference, ConcreteDecoratorA and ConcreteDecoratorB extending Decorator. Show wrapping relationship with nested boxes visualization.

slides.speakerNotes: Decorator adds behavior to objects dynamically without subclassing. Decorator implements same interface as component it wraps and contains reference to component. It forwards requests to wrapped component, adding behavior before/after. Multiple decorators can be chained. Classic example: Java I/O streams—BufferedInputStream wraps FileInputStream, which might wrap another stream. Coffee shop analogy: plain coffee decorated with milk, sugar, whipped cream. Each decorator adds cost and functionality.

slides.title: Decorator Implementation: Design Challenge

content.title: Apply: Complete the Decorator
content.instructions: Implement CompressionDecorator following the pattern structure. Then answer: How would you stack EncryptionDecorator and CompressionDecorator? Which order (compress-then-encrypt or encrypt-then-compress) and why? Consider data size and security implications.
content.deliverable: Sketch class structure; justify decorator ordering with rationale

items: When would Decorator be better than subclassing?
What problems arise with too many decorators?
How does order affect behavior and performance?

slides.speakerNotes: Students implement CompressionDecorator applying pattern structure from slide 14, then evaluate decorator ordering trade-offs. Compression-then-encryption reduces encrypted data size but encryption-then-compression may leak information through compression ratios. Discuss when Decorator beats inheritance (runtime flexibility, avoiding class explosion) versus drawbacks (debugging complexity, many small objects, identity issues). Poll students on ordering choice before revealing that security typically trumps efficiency. This bridges apply (implementation) and evaluate (justify ordering) levels, directly supporting objectives requiring pattern application and selection based on trade-offs.

slides.title: Pattern Selection Criteria

items: Identify the design problem and forces
Compile-time vs. runtime flexibility needs
Coupling and cohesion implications
Complexity cost vs. flexibility benefit
Team familiarity and maintainability

blocks.content: Patterns are not always the answer: YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It)

slides.speakerNotes: Selecting the right pattern requires analyzing the specific problem. Consider: Do you need compile-time or runtime flexibility? How much coupling can you tolerate? Is the added complexity justified by the flexibility gained? Can your team maintain pattern-based code? Multiple patterns may solve the same problem differently—choose based on trade-offs. Important warning: don't over-engineer. Apply patterns when you have a real problem they solve, not speculatively. YAGNI principle: implement what you need now, not what you might need later. Premature abstraction is as bad as premature optimization.

slides.title: Patterns in Real-World Systems

items: Java Collections: Iterator, Factory Method, Composite
Spring Framework: Singleton, Factory, Proxy, Template Method
GUI Frameworks: Composite, Decorator, Observer, Strategy
Patterns rarely appear in isolation
Refactoring to patterns vs. upfront design

content.prompt: Architecture diagram showing a web application framework with boxes representing different components, labeled with patterns they use: Controller (Factory Method), View (Composite), Model (Observer), Middleware (Decorator), Database (Abstract Factory, Singleton). Show connections between components.

slides.speakerNotes: Real systems use multiple patterns working together. Java Collections Framework: Collection.iterator() is Factory Method, List/Set hierarchies use Composite-like structure. Spring uses Singleton for beans, Factory for bean creation, Proxy for AOP. GUI frameworks are pattern-rich: widget hierarchies (Composite), widget decoration (Decorator), event handling (Observer). Important distinction: refactoring to patterns (evolving simple code as complexity grows) vs. designing with patterns upfront. Fowler advocates refactoring approach—start simple, introduce patterns when needed. Recognize patterns in existing code to understand architecture faster.

slides.title: Summary and Next Steps

items: Creational: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory
Structural: Adapter, Composite, Decorator
Patterns embody OO principles: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism
Selection depends on specific forces and trade-offs

blocks.content: Next Lecture: Behavioral Patterns (Observer, Strategy, Visitor, Template Method)

items: Complete tutorial: implement each pattern
Portfolio: design system using 3+ patterns with justification
Read ahead: Observer and Strategy patterns

slides.speakerNotes: Recap: We covered 6 fundamental patterns today. Creational patterns control object creation—Singleton for single instances, Factory Method for subclass-based creation, Abstract Factory for product families. Structural patterns organize composition—Adapter for interface conversion, Composite for tree structures, Decorator for dynamic behavior addition. These patterns embody core OO principles and provide vocabulary for design discussions. Next lecture covers behavioral patterns focusing on object interaction and responsibility distribution. Action items: implement each pattern in tutorial exercises, start portfolio assignment using multiple patterns with written justification, read about Observer and Strategy to prepare. Emphasize connection to ILO 4: applying fundamental design patterns to build high-quality, extendible systems.

objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 4-9 systematically present all three creational patterns with implementation activities. objectiveAlignments.objective: Apply structural patterns (Adapter, Composite, Decorator) to organize class and object composition
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 10-15 cover all three structural patterns with hands-on application. objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 5, 6, 11, 13, 15, and 16 engage evaluation through trade-off analysis and pattern selection justification. Emphasize no universally correct answer; optimal choice depends on anticipated change, team context, and complexity tolerance. This addresses objective 4's evaluate-level demand through direct pattern comparison rather than isolated analysis.

slides.title: Factory Method: Apply & Evaluate Alternatives

content.title: Implement & Evaluate Pattern Alternatives
content.instructions: Logistics system needs Air transport support. (1) Implement AirLogistics using Factory Method pattern (2 min). (2) Redesign the same extension using a static factory with switch statement (2 min). (3) Evaluate both: Which better supports adding Ship transport next sprint? Which simplifies unit testing Transport types independently? If requirements are stable with only 3 transport types ever, which approach is justified? Defend your selection with specific trade-offs.
content.format: Individual implementation, then pair debate comparing both approaches

items: Compare: Modification points when adding new transport types
Analyze: Testing isolation—mocking factories vs. conditional logic
Evaluate: Does parallel hierarchy justify complexity for this context?
Justify: Pattern selection requires anticipated change vs. current need

slides.speakerNotes: This slide elevates cognitive demand by requiring students to implement the same solution with two competing approaches, then evaluate which is optimal for specific contexts. Push students beyond 'Factory Method is better' to justified selection: Factory Method wins for extensibility and testability but over-engineers stable requirements; static factory balances simplicity with moderate extension. During pair debate, challenge defenses with counterarguments about YAGNI principle and premature abstraction. Connect to slide 6's notification system showing similar evaluation. Emphasize context-dependent selection addresses objective 4's evaluate-level demand through direct pattern comparison.

slides.title: Abstract Factory: Creating Product Families

items: Intent: Create families of related objects
Ensures products work together
Multiple creation methods per factory
Client uses abstract interfaces only

content.prompt: UML diagram showing AbstractFactory interface with createProductA() and createProductB() methods, ConcreteFactory1 and ConcreteFactory2 implementing it, AbstractProductA and AbstractProductB interfaces, and concrete products ProductA1, ProductA2, ProductB1, ProductB2. Use different colors for each product family.

slides.speakerNotes: Abstract Factory creates families of related objects. Key difference from Factory Method: creates multiple product types that must work together. Classic example: UI toolkit creating Button, Checkbox, ScrollBar for Windows/Mac/Linux—products from same family share consistent look. The factory interface declares creation methods for each product type. Concrete factories return compatible products. Client code works only with abstract interfaces, never concrete classes.

slides.title: Abstract Factory vs Factory Method: Pattern Selection

content.title: Pattern Selection Challenge
content.instructions: Scenario: You're building a document editor supporting PDF and Word formats. Each format needs a DocumentParser and ImageExtractor that work together consistently. Which pattern? Justify your choice by analyzing: (1) number of product types, (2) consistency requirements, (3) extensibility needs for adding formats vs. adding operations.
content.deliverable: Pattern choice with 3-point justification addressing trade-offs

slides.speakerNotes: This comparison enables pattern selection decisions. Key distinction: Factory Method uses inheritance for single products; Abstract Factory uses composition for product families. The activity requires evaluating both patterns against specific requirements. Students must analyze the scenario's two product types (parser, extractor) that need consistency, then justify why Abstract Factory's family-creation strength outweighs its limitation when adding new product types. This evaluate-level task addresses objective 4 by requiring justified selection between competing patterns based on design forces and trade-offs.

slides.title: Adapter Pattern: Interface Conversion

items: Intent: Convert incompatible interfaces
Wraps existing class with new interface
Two variants: Class and Object Adapter
Enables reuse without modification

content.prompt: UML diagram showing Client using Target interface, Adapter implementing Target and containing Adaptee reference, and Adaptee class with incompatible interface. Show delegation arrow from Adapter to Adaptee with 'adaptee.specificRequest()' label.

slides.speakerNotes: Adapter makes incompatible interfaces work together—like a power adapter converting US plug to European socket. The Adapter implements the interface the client expects (Target) and wraps the existing class (Adaptee). Object Adapter uses composition (shown here)—more flexible, can adapt multiple adaptees. Class Adapter uses multiple inheritance—more efficient but less flexible. Real example: Java's InputStreamReader adapts byte streams to character streams. Use when you can't modify existing code but need it to work with new interface.

slides.title: Adapter Pattern: Evaluate & Create Solutions

content.text:
**Design Challenge**: Your system uses `Logger` interface with `log(String msg)`. A third-party library provides `AdvancedLogger` with `writeLog(String msg, LogLevel level, Timestamp time)`. You need structured logging but can't modify either interface.

**Competing Solutions**: (1) Adapter with hardcoded defaults, (2) Adapter parsing message for level hints, (3) Wrapper adding setLevel() method, (4) Abandon Logger interface entirely.

**Your Task**: Evaluate which solution best fits if clients need occasional level control but mostly default INFO logging.

content.instructions: 1. Individually: Rank the 4 solutions by appropriateness. Justify using OO principles (encapsulation, LSP) and pattern intent (1.5 min). 2. Pair: Compare rankings—what criteria drove your decisions? Identify where solutions violate Adapter pattern vs. becoming different patterns (1.5 min). 3. Create: Propose hybrid solution combining strengths of top 2 approaches (1 min).

slides.speakerNotes: This evaluate-level activity requires students to compare competing solutions against pattern intent and OO principles, not just implement one approach. Key insight: solution 3 violates Adapter pattern (changes Target interface), solution 4 abandons the constraint. During pair work, surface that parsing (solution 2) breaks encapsulation while defaults (solution 1) lose flexibility. The create phase scaffolds synthesis: best hybrid often adds optional configuration to adapter constructor while maintaining Logger interface. Debrief connects to objective 4—pattern selection requires evaluating trade-offs across multiple candidate solutions, not just analyzing one pattern's limitations. Emphasize when to adapt vs. when constraint itself is wrong.

slides.title: Composite Pattern: Part-Whole Hierarchies

items: Intent: Compose objects into tree structures
Treat individual and composite objects uniformly
Recursive composition
Component, Leaf, Composite roles

content.prompt: UML diagram showing Component interface with operation(), Leaf implementing Component, and Composite implementing Component with children list and add/remove methods. Show tree structure with Composite containing both Leaf and other Composite objects.

slides.speakerNotes: Composite represents part-whole hierarchies as trees. Classic example: file system with files (leaves) and directories (composites containing files and other directories). The key insight: clients treat leaves and composites uniformly through Component interface. Composite stores children and delegates operations to them recursively. This enables building complex structures from simple parts. The pattern embodies recursion—composites can contain other composites. GUI frameworks use this extensively: panels contain buttons, labels, and other panels.

slides.title: Composite Pattern: Implementation Challenge

content.title: Apply & Analyze (3 min)
content.instructions:
1. Complete the draw() method using recursive delegation
2. Decide: Should add/remove methods be in Graphic interface or only CompositeGraphic?
3. Justify your choice: What are the trade-offs?

Consider: What happens if client calls add() on a Circle?
content.deliverable: Code completion + design decision with rationale

slides.speakerNotes: This active learning exercise elevates engagement to apply and analyze levels. Students first apply the pattern by implementing recursive delegation, then analyze the transparency vs. safety trade-off. Poll students on their interface decision. Transparency (add/remove in Graphic) treats all objects uniformly but allows unsafe operations on leaves. Safety (add/remove only in Composite) prevents errors but requires type checking. Discuss how different contexts favor different approaches: GUI frameworks often choose transparency, while type-safe systems prefer safety. Connect to real design decisions they'll face.

slides.title: Decorator Pattern: Dynamic Responsibilities

items: Intent: Add responsibilities dynamically
Flexible alternative to subclassing
Decorator wraps component
Multiple decorators can be stacked

content.prompt: UML diagram showing Component interface, ConcreteComponent implementing it, Decorator implementing Component and containing Component reference, ConcreteDecoratorA and ConcreteDecoratorB extending Decorator. Show wrapping relationship with nested boxes visualization.

slides.speakerNotes: Decorator adds behavior to objects dynamically without subclassing. Decorator implements same interface as component it wraps and contains reference to component. It forwards requests to wrapped component, adding behavior before/after. Multiple decorators can be chained. Classic example: Java I/O streams—BufferedInputStream wraps FileInputStream, which might wrap another stream. Coffee shop analogy: plain coffee decorated with milk, sugar, whipped cream. Each decorator adds cost and functionality.

slides.title: Decorator Implementation: Design Challenge

content.title: Apply: Complete the Decorator
content.instructions: Implement CompressionDecorator following the pattern structure. Then answer: How would you stack EncryptionDecorator and CompressionDecorator? Which order (compress-then-encrypt or encrypt-then-compress) and why? Consider data size and security implications.
content.deliverable: Sketch class structure; justify decorator ordering with rationale

items: When would Decorator be better than subclassing?
What problems arise with too many decorators?
How does order affect behavior and performance?

slides.speakerNotes: Students implement CompressionDecorator applying pattern structure from slide 14, then evaluate decorator ordering trade-offs. Compression-then-encryption reduces encrypted data size but encryption-then-compression may leak information through compression ratios. Discuss when Decorator beats inheritance (runtime flexibility, avoiding class explosion) versus drawbacks (debugging complexity, many small objects, identity issues). Poll students on ordering choice before revealing that security typically trumps efficiency. This bridges apply (implementation) and evaluate (justify ordering) levels, directly supporting objectives requiring pattern application and selection based on trade-offs.

slides.title: Pattern Selection: Apply the Criteria

content.title: Design Challenge
content.description: You need to add logging to 15+ classes in a legacy system. Logs must include timestamps, user context, and be filterable by severity. Requirements may change (add encryption, remote logging).
content.question: Which approach and why?
options: B. Decorator: Wrap objects with LoggingDecorator
C. Proxy: Create logging proxies for each class

content.title: Evaluate: Justify Your Pattern Choice
content.instructions: Select approach A, B, or C. Apply selection criteria: runtime flexibility needs, coupling impact, extensibility for new features (encryption, remote logging), and maintenance complexity. Justify your choice against the alternatives, identifying which criteria matter most for this scenario.
content.deliverable: Written justification citing at least 3 criteria; explain why rejected alternatives fail

items: Runtime flexibility: Can behavior change without recompilation?
Extensibility: How easily can new features stack?
Coupling: Does solution force dependencies on existing classes?
Complexity vs. benefit: Is added abstraction justified?

slides.speakerNotes: Students evaluate three competing solutions using explicit criteria. Inheritance creates tight coupling, limits runtime changes, and doesn't support stacking features. Proxy requires creating 15+ proxy classes, high maintenance cost. Decorator offers runtime composition, supports stacking (logging + encryption), minimal coupling, but adds object overhead. Poll class on choices before discussion. Reveal that Decorator best fits extensibility and runtime flexibility needs despite complexity. Emphasize trade-off thinking: no perfect answer, but justified selection based on prioritized criteria. This directly targets objective 4 (evaluate and select) at evaluate level, moving beyond conceptual criteria to applied decision-making.

slides.title: Pattern Recognition in Real Systems

content.title: Identify Patterns and Analyze Collaboration
content.instructions: Examine the code. Identify at least 3 patterns used. For each: name the pattern, cite specific evidence (lines/methods), and explain how patterns collaborate. Then evaluate: which pattern could be eliminated if requirements simplified to single logger type? Justify your answer.
content.deliverable: List of patterns with evidence; analysis of how they work together; justified evaluation of which is least essential

items: Patterns: Singleton (WebApp instance), Abstract/Factory Method (LoggerFactory), Decorator (wrapping loggers)
Collaboration: Singleton manages factory; factory creates objects for Decorator chain
Recognition skill: Identify patterns in unfamiliar codebases to understand architecture faster

slides.speakerNotes: Students analyze real code to identify patterns and their interactions—moving from understanding examples to analyzing unfamiliar implementations. Code shows Singleton (getInstance), Factory Method (createLogger/logFactory), Decorator (TimestampDecorator wrapping FilterDecorator). Patterns collaborate: Singleton provides single factory instance, factory creates base logger, decorators add behavior dynamically. Evaluation question targets objective 4: which pattern is least essential? Factory could be eliminated if only one logger type exists, but Singleton and Decorator provide distinct value. Poll students, discuss justifications. This develops pattern recognition in real systems and evaluates appropriateness based on requirements—key professional skills.

slides.title: Summary and Next Steps

items: Creational: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory
Structural: Adapter, Composite, Decorator
Patterns embody OO principles: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism
Selection depends on specific forces and trade-offs

blocks.content: Next Lecture: Behavioral Patterns (Observer, Strategy, Visitor, Template Method)

items: Complete tutorial: implement each pattern
Portfolio: design system using 3+ patterns with justification
Read ahead: Observer and Strategy patterns

These patterns embody core OO principles and provide vocabulary for design discussions. Next lecture covers behavioral patterns focusing on object interaction and responsibility distribution. Emphasize connection to ILO 4: applying fundamental design patterns to build high-quality, extendible systems.

slides.title: What Are Design Patterns?

blocks.content: Reusable solutions to commonly occurring problems in software design—templates capturing expert knowledge, not finished code. Patterns provide shared vocabulary and leverage OO principles (encapsulation, polymorphism, composition).

content.title: Recognize Patterns in Real Code
content.instructions: Examine these Java framework examples: (1) Collections.unmodifiableList(list) wraps a list to prevent modification. content.title: Implement Product Families
content.instructions: Build DocumentFactory creating Parser and ImageExtractor families for PDF and Word formats. (1) IMPLEMENT: Code AbstractFactory interface with createParser() and createExtractor() methods, then PDFFactory and WordFactory concrete implementations (3 min). (2) EXTEND: Add RTFFactory supporting RTF format (2 min). (3) ANALYZE: What code changed when adding RTF? Compare to adding a new product type (FontRenderer) across all factories.
content.deliverable: Working factory code showing family extension vs. product extension trade-offs

items: ANALYZE: Which is easier—adding RTF family or adding FontRenderer product? Why?
EVALUATE: When does family consistency justify Abstract Factory's product-extension cost?
Products must work together (PDF parser + PDF extractor, not mixed)

slides.speakerNotes: This activity provides apply-level implementation practice for Abstract Factory, balancing hands-on coding across all creational patterns per gap analysis. Students implement the factory interface and two concrete families, then extend with RTF to experience easy family addition. The analysis phase reveals Abstract Factory's core trade-off: simple family extension but difficult product-type addition (adding FontRenderer requires changing all factories). During debrief, contrast with Factory Method's opposite trade-off. Collect examples showing students recognized when family consistency requirements justify this design choice, strengthening pattern selection skills.

slides.title: Abstract Factory vs Factory Method: Pattern Selection

content.title: Implement & Justify Pattern Choice
content.instructions: Document editor needs PDF and Word support. Each format requires Parser and ImageExtractor working together. (1) IMPLEMENT: Code AbstractFactory with createParser() and createExtractor(), plus PDFFactory and WordFactory (4 min). (2) EXTEND: Add RTF format support (1 min). (3) CREATE: Propose alternative using Factory Method for parsers and extractors separately. (4) EVALUATE: Compare both designs—which better handles adding formats vs. adding new product types like FontRenderer? Justify final choice.
content.deliverable: Working code for both approaches with justified selection based on extensibility trade-offs

slides.speakerNotes: This activity balances apply-level implementation with create-level design synthesis and evaluate-level justification. Students implement Abstract Factory experiencing easy family extension (RTF), then design an alternative using separate Factory Methods. The comparison reveals Abstract Factory's strength (family consistency) versus its weakness (hard to add product types). During debrief, emphasize when family cohesion requirements justify Abstract Factory's constraints. This addresses the gap in Abstract Factory hands-on practice while engaging create-level by requiring students to generate and compare alternative designs rather than selecting from pre-defined options.

slides.title: Adapter Pattern: Interface Conversion

items: Intent: Convert incompatible interfaces
Wraps existing class with new interface
Two variants: Class and Object Adapter
Enables reuse without modification

content.prompt: UML diagram showing Client using Target interface, Adapter implementing Target and containing Adaptee reference, and Adaptee class with incompatible interface. Show delegation arrow from Adapter to Adaptee with 'adaptee.specificRequest()' label.

slides.speakerNotes: Adapter makes incompatible interfaces work together—like a power adapter converting US plug to European socket. The Adapter implements the interface the client expects (Target) and wraps the existing class (Adaptee). Object Adapter uses composition (shown here)—more flexible, can adapt multiple adaptees. Class Adapter uses multiple inheritance—more efficient but less flexible. Real example: Java's InputStreamReader adapts byte streams to character streams. Use when you can't modify existing code but need it to work with new interface.

slides.title: Adapter Pattern: Evaluate & Create Solutions

content.text:
**Design Challenge**: Your system uses `Logger` interface with `log(String msg)`. A third-party library provides `AdvancedLogger` with `writeLog(String msg, LogLevel level, Timestamp time)`. You need structured logging but can't modify either interface.

**Competing Solutions**: (1) Adapter with hardcoded defaults, (2) Adapter parsing message for level hints, (3) Wrapper adding setLevel() method, (4) Abandon Logger interface entirely.

**Your Task**: Evaluate which solution best fits if clients need occasional level control but mostly default INFO logging.

content.instructions: 1. Individually: Rank the 4 solutions by appropriateness. Justify using OO principles (encapsulation, LSP) and pattern intent (1.5 min). 2. Pair: Compare rankings—what criteria drove your decisions? Identify where solutions violate Adapter pattern vs. becoming different patterns (1.5 min). 3. Create: Propose hybrid solution combining strengths of top 2 approaches (1 min).

slides.speakerNotes: This evaluate-level activity requires students to compare competing solutions against pattern intent and OO principles, not just implement one approach. Key insight: solution 3 violates Adapter pattern (changes Target interface), solution 4 abandons the constraint. During pair work, surface that parsing (solution 2) breaks encapsulation while defaults (solution 1) lose flexibility. The create phase scaffolds synthesis: best hybrid often adds optional configuration to adapter constructor while maintaining Logger interface. Debrief connects to objective 4—pattern selection requires evaluating trade-offs across multiple candidate solutions, not just analyzing one pattern's limitations. Emphasize when to adapt vs. when constraint itself is wrong.

slides.title: Composite Pattern: Part-Whole Hierarchies

items: Intent: Compose objects into tree structures
Treat individual and composite objects uniformly
Recursive composition
Component, Leaf, Composite roles

content.prompt: UML diagram showing Component interface with operation(), Leaf implementing Component, and Composite implementing Component with children list and add/remove methods. Show tree structure with Composite containing both Leaf and other Composite objects.

slides.speakerNotes: Composite represents part-whole hierarchies as trees. Classic example: file system with files (leaves) and directories (composites containing files and other directories). The key insight: clients treat leaves and composites uniformly through Component interface. Composite stores children and delegates operations to them recursively. This enables building complex structures from simple parts. The pattern embodies recursion—composites can contain other composites. GUI frameworks use this extensively: panels contain buttons, labels, and other panels.

slides.title: Composite Pattern: Implementation Challenge

content.title: Apply & Analyze (3 min)
content.instructions:
1. Complete the draw() method using recursive delegation
2. Decide: Should add/remove methods be in Graphic interface or only CompositeGraphic?
3. Justify your choice: What are the trade-offs?

Consider: What happens if client calls add() on a Circle?
content.deliverable: Code completion + design decision with rationale

slides.speakerNotes: This active learning exercise elevates engagement to apply and analyze levels. Students first apply the pattern by implementing recursive delegation, then analyze the transparency vs. safety trade-off. Poll students on their interface decision. Transparency (add/remove in Graphic) treats all objects uniformly but allows unsafe operations on leaves. Safety (add/remove only in Composite) prevents errors but requires type checking. Discuss how different contexts favor different approaches: GUI frameworks often choose transparency, while type-safe systems prefer safety. Connect to real design decisions they'll face.

slides.title: Decorator Pattern: Dynamic Responsibilities

items: Intent: Add responsibilities dynamically
Flexible alternative to subclassing
Decorator wraps component
Multiple decorators can be stacked

content.prompt: UML diagram showing Component interface, ConcreteComponent implementing it, Decorator implementing Component and containing Component reference, ConcreteDecoratorA and ConcreteDecoratorB extending Decorator. Show wrapping relationship with nested boxes visualization.

slides.speakerNotes: Decorator adds behavior to objects dynamically without subclassing. Decorator implements same interface as component it wraps and contains reference to component. It forwards requests to wrapped component, adding behavior before/after. Multiple decorators can be chained. Classic example: Java I/O streams—BufferedInputStream wraps FileInputStream, which might wrap another stream. Coffee shop analogy: plain coffee decorated with milk, sugar, whipped cream. Each decorator adds cost and functionality.

slides.title: Decorator Implementation: Design Challenge

content.title: Apply: Complete the Decorator
content.instructions: Implement CompressionDecorator following the pattern structure. Then answer: How would you stack EncryptionDecorator and CompressionDecorator? Which order (compress-then-encrypt or encrypt-then-compress) and why? Consider data size and security implications.
content.deliverable: Sketch class structure; justify decorator ordering with rationale

items: When would Decorator be better than subclassing?
What problems arise with too many decorators?
How does order affect behavior and performance?

slides.speakerNotes: Students implement CompressionDecorator applying pattern structure from slide 14, then evaluate decorator ordering trade-offs. Compression-then-encryption reduces encrypted data size but encryption-then-compression may leak information through compression ratios. Discuss when Decorator beats inheritance (runtime flexibility, avoiding class explosion) versus drawbacks (debugging complexity, many small objects, identity issues). Poll students on ordering choice before revealing that security typically trumps efficiency. This bridges apply (implementation) and evaluate (justify ordering) levels, directly supporting objectives requiring pattern application and selection based on trade-offs.

slides.title: Pattern Selection: Apply the Criteria

content.title: Design Challenge
content.description: You need to add logging to 15+ classes in a legacy system. Logs must include timestamps, user context, and be filterable by severity. Requirements may change (add encryption, remote logging).
content.question: Which approach and why?
options: B. Decorator: Wrap objects with LoggingDecorator
C. Proxy: Create logging proxies for each class

content.title: Evaluate: Justify Your Pattern Choice
content.instructions: Select approach A, B, or C. Apply selection criteria: runtime flexibility needs, coupling impact, extensibility for new features (encryption, remote logging), and maintenance complexity. Justify your choice against the alternatives, identifying which criteria matter most for this scenario.
content.deliverable: Written justification citing at least 3 criteria; explain why rejected alternatives fail

items: Runtime flexibility: Can behavior change without recompilation?
Extensibility: How easily can new features stack?
Coupling: Does solution force dependencies on existing classes?
Complexity vs. benefit: Is added abstraction justified?

slides.speakerNotes: Students evaluate three competing solutions using explicit criteria. Inheritance creates tight coupling, limits runtime changes, and doesn't support stacking features. Proxy requires creating 15+ proxy classes, high maintenance cost. Decorator offers runtime composition, supports stacking (logging + encryption), minimal coupling, but adds object overhead. Poll class on choices before discussion. Reveal that Decorator best fits extensibility and runtime flexibility needs despite complexity. Emphasize trade-off thinking: no perfect answer, but justified selection based on prioritized criteria. This directly targets objective 4 (evaluate and select) at evaluate level, moving beyond conceptual criteria to applied decision-making.

slides.title: Pattern Recognition in Real Systems

content.title: Identify Patterns and Analyze Collaboration
content.instructions: Examine the code. Identify at least 3 patterns used. For each: name the pattern, cite specific evidence (lines/methods), and explain how patterns collaborate. Then evaluate: which pattern could be eliminated if requirements simplified to single logger type? Justify your answer.
content.deliverable: List of patterns with evidence; analysis of how they work together; justified evaluation of which is least essential

items: Patterns: Singleton (WebApp instance), Abstract/Factory Method (LoggerFactory), Decorator (wrapping loggers)
Collaboration: Singleton manages factory; factory creates objects for Decorator chain
Recognition skill: Identify patterns in unfamiliar codebases to understand architecture faster

slides.speakerNotes: Students analyze real code to identify patterns and their interactions—moving from understanding examples to analyzing unfamiliar implementations. Code shows Singleton (getInstance), Factory Method (createLogger/logFactory), Decorator (TimestampDecorator wrapping FilterDecorator). Patterns collaborate: Singleton provides single factory instance, factory creates base logger, decorators add behavior dynamically. Evaluation question targets objective 4: which pattern is least essential? Factory could be eliminated if only one logger type exists, but Singleton and Decorator provide distinct value. Poll students, discuss justifications. This develops pattern recognition in real systems and evaluates appropriateness based on requirements—key professional skills.

slides.title: Summary and Next Steps

items: Creational: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory
Structural: Adapter, Composite, Decorator
Patterns embody OO principles: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism
Selection depends on specific forces and trade-offs

slides.speakerNotes: Recap: We covered 6 fundamental patterns today. Creational patterns control object creation—Singleton for single instances, Factory Method for subclass-based creation, Abstract Factory for product families. Structural patterns organize composition—Adapter for interface conversion, Composite for tree structures, Decorator for dynamic behavior addition. These patterns embody core OO principles and provide vocabulary for design discussions. Next lecture covers behavioral patterns focusing on object interaction and responsibility distribution. Action items: implement each pattern in tutorial exercises, start portfolio assignment using multiple patterns with written justification, read about Observer and Strategy to prepare. Emphasize connection to ILO 4: applying fundamental design patterns to build high-quality, extendible systems.
